name: AI for Business Productivity
objectives: Given a messy list of next week's tasks, use AI to group them and create a time-blocked week plan with your own top three priorities, with the plan entered in your calendar
Given today's inbox, sort email into groups and send AI-drafted replies that you check first, with no private customer details pasted into the AI
Given your three most-asked customer questions, create a reusable reply template for each with blanks to fill in, with your real facts checked and the templates saved where you can reach them
Given a job you repeat every week, write a numbered step-by-step procedure with a checklist, tested once by following it word for word and fixed
Given a long business document with private details removed, get an AI summary of dates, fees and duties and compare it with the original, reading the money and legal parts yourself
For one task you do every week, log your time before and after using AI and calculate the weekly minutes saved, counting the time spent checking and fixing AI's work

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Planning your week by priority
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to turn a messy to-do list into a week plan with three priorities.
This lesson builds toward: Given a messy list of next week's tasks, you will use AI to group them and create a time-blocked week plan with your own top three priorities, with the plan entered in your calendar.
A long to-do list hides what matters. AI is good at sorting. Paste in your list (no private customer details) and ask it to group tasks and suggest which three will most help your business this week.
A simple way to judge: tasks that bring in money or keep customers happy usually come first; tasks that can wait or be handed off come later. You decide the final order, because you know your business.
Then ask for a time-blocked plan: "Put these into my week. I work 8 am to 4 pm, Monday to Friday, and do deliveries on Tuesday and Thursday mornings." Put the plan into your calendar.
Step by step:
- Write every task in your head as a list.
- Ask AI to group the tasks and suggest the top three for the week.
- Pick your own top three.
- Ask AI to place the tasks into time blocks around your fixed hours.
- Copy the blocks into your calendar.
Words to know:
- Priority: a task that matters most right now.
- Time block: a set period on your calendar for one kind of work.
Try it now: Write your full task list for next week, ask an AI assistant to group it and suggest a top three, choose your own top three, and get a time-blocked plan you put in your calendar.
You can now turn a messy list into a week plan with clear priorities and time blocks.

options: A set period on your calendar for one kind of work
check.why: Time blocks protect time for your priorities.

check.q: AI suggests your top three tasks, but one is a low-value chore. What do you do?
check.why: You decide the final priorities; AI only suggests.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Clearing your inbox faster
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to sort emails and draft replies you check before sending.
This lesson builds toward: Given today's inbox, you will sort email into groups and send AI-drafted replies that you check first, with no private customer details pasted into the AI.
Email eats hours. Sort it first: reply now (customers, money, urgent), reply later, read only, and delete or unsubscribe. Many email apps can also filter messages automatically into folders or labels.
For replies, AI can turn your quick notes into a polite message: "Reply to a customer asking to move their Friday booking. Say yes, offer Saturday 10 am or Monday 2 pm, and keep it short and warm." Gmail and Outlook may also offer built-in AI suggestions depending on your plan.
Never paste a customer's full email with their phone number, address or card details into a chat tool. Summarize the question in your own words instead. And always read a reply before you send it.
Step by step:
- Sort your inbox into: reply now, reply later, read only, delete.
- For each reply-now email, write a one-line note of what you want to say.
- Ask AI to turn the note into a short reply.
- Read, fix and send it yourself.
Words to know:
- Filter: an email rule that moves messages into a folder or label automatically.
- Unsubscribe: the link that stops a company emailing you.
Try it now: Sort today's inbox into the four groups. For two reply-now emails, write a one-line note, have AI draft the reply, check it and send it. Time how long it took.
You can now sort email by importance and send faster, checked replies with AI's help.

check.q: Which emails belong in the reply-now group?
check.why: Reply-now emails affect customers and money.

check.q: AI drafts a reply to a customer. What do you do before sending?
options: Read it and fix anything wrong
check.why: You check every AI draft before it goes out under your name.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reusable templates for messages you write again and again
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Create three reply templates for the questions customers ask most.
This lesson builds toward: Given your three most-asked customer questions, you will create a reusable reply template for each with blanks to fill in, with your real facts checked and the templates saved where you can reach them.
If you answer the same question every week (prices, hours, how to book, refund policy), write the answer once and reuse it. AI can help you write a clear, friendly template.
A good template has blanks you fill in: "Hi [name], thanks for asking about [service]. Our price for [size] is [price]. You can book at [link or number]." Keep your real facts in the template, and check them whenever prices or policies change.
Save templates where you can grab them fast: a document, your phone's notes app, or the saved-reply feature many email apps and business messaging apps offer.
Step by step:
- List the five questions customers ask most.
- Pick the top three.
- Ask AI for a short, friendly template for each with [blanks].
- Fill in your real facts and check them.
- Save the templates where you can reach them quickly.
Words to know:
- Template: a ready-made message with blanks you fill in each time.
- Saved reply: an email or messaging feature that stores a template for one-click use.
Try it now: Write down your three most-asked customer questions and use AI to make a template for each. Fill in your real facts and save them.
You can now write and reuse templates for the customer questions you answer most.

check.q: What are the blanks like [name] in a template for?
options: Details you fill in each time
check.why: Blanks let you reuse one template for many customers.

check.q: You changed your opening hours. What do you do with your templates?
options: Update and recheck every template that mentions hours
Wait for a customer to complain
check.why: Templates must match your current facts.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a standard operating procedure
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn one job you repeat into a written step-by-step procedure with AI.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job you repeat every week, you will write a numbered step-by-step procedure with a checklist, tested once by following it word for word and fixed.
A standard operating procedure (SOP) is a written list of steps for doing a job the same way every time. It lets a helper do the job without calling you, and it stops mistakes when you are busy.
Easy way to make one: do the job once while saying or typing each step in rough notes. Then ask AI: "Turn these notes into a clear numbered procedure a new helper can follow. Add a short checklist at the end."
Test the SOP: give it to someone (or follow it yourself, word for word) and fix any step that was confusing or missing.
Step by step:
- Choose a job you repeat every week, such as opening the shop or packing an order.
- Do it once while writing rough notes of each step.
- Ask AI to turn the notes into a numbered procedure and checklist.
- Test it by following it exactly, or have a helper try.
- Fix unclear steps and save the final version.
Words to know:
- SOP: standard operating procedure: written steps for doing a job the same way every time.
- Checklist: a short list you tick off to be sure nothing was missed.
Try it now: Pick one weekly job, write rough notes while you do it, and have AI turn them into a numbered SOP with a checklist. Test it once and fix it.
You can now turn a repeated job into a tested, written procedure.

check.q: What does a standard operating procedure (SOP) do?
options: Writes down the steps of a repeated job so anyone can do it the same way
check.why: An SOP lets a helper do the job without calling you.

check.q: Your helper follows your new SOP and gets stuck at step 4. What do you do?
options: Fix step 4 so it is clear and test again
check.why: Testing shows where a procedure needs fixing.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Summaries and quick research
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Use AI to summarize long documents and do quick, checked research.
This lesson builds toward: Given a long business document with private details removed, you will get an AI summary of dates, fees and duties and compare it with the original, reading the money and legal parts yourself.
Business owners get long documents: supplier terms, grant rules, lease drafts, reports. AI can summarize them: "Summarize this in 8 bullet points. List any dates, fees or things I must do." Remove private details first, and read the original parts that matter, especially anything about money or legal duties.
AI can also speed up research: comparing suppliers, explaining a new term, or listing questions to ask an accountant. Ask it for sources, then open those sources yourself.
For legal, tax or license questions, use AI to prepare good questions, then get the answer from the official agency site or a professional.
Step by step:
- Remove private details from the document.
- Ask for a short summary plus dates, fees and duties.
- Read the original sections about money or legal duties.
- For research, ask for sources and open them yourself.
Words to know:
- Summary: a short version that keeps the main points.
- Terms: the rules and conditions in an agreement.
Try it now: Take a long business document you have (with private details removed), ask AI for an 8-bullet summary with dates, fees and duties, and compare it with the original.
You can now get a fast, checked summary of a long business document.

check.q: What should a good summary request ask for?
options: Main points plus dates, fees and duties
check.why: Dates, fees and duties are what an owner must act on.

check.q: AI summarizes your lease and says there is no late fee. What do you do?
options: Check the money section of the lease yourself
Ask AI the same question again
check.why: You read the money and legal parts yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measuring the time you save
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Log your time before and after using AI on one task to see if it really helps.
This lesson builds toward: For one task you do every week, you will log your time before and after using AI and calculate the weekly minutes saved, counting the time spent checking and fixing AI's work.
AI should save you time, not just feel busy. Measure it. Pick one task, such as answering booking questions or writing the weekly post. Write down how long it takes the old way, then how long it takes with AI, including the time to check and fix.
Multiply: minutes saved per time, times how many times a week. Ten minutes saved on a task you do 15 times a week is 150 minutes, two and a half hours.
If a task is not faster with AI, or needs so much fixing that it is not worth it, stop using AI for that task. Put the saved time into the tasks that grow your business.
Step by step:
- Choose one task you do often.
- Time it the old way once.
- Time it with AI, including checking and fixing.
- Multiply the minutes saved by how often you do it each week.
- Keep, change or drop AI for that task.
Words to know:
- Time log: a simple record of how long tasks take.
Try it now: Final task: build your time-back kit: your AI-planned week, your three templates, your SOP, and a before-and-after time log for one task with the weekly minutes saved.
You can now prove whether AI saves you time and decide where to use it in your business.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Week plan No priorities chosen, or the plan is not in the calendar. Three priorities chosen by the owner and time blocks in the calendar. The top three link clearly to money or customers, and fixed jobs are blocked first. Reply templates Fewer than three templates, or facts are wrong. Three templates with blanks and checked facts, saved where they are easy to reach. Templates are already in use and have been updated once. Procedure Steps are missing or the SOP was not tested. Numbered steps and a checklist, tested once and fixed. A helper followed it without asking questions. Time log No before-and-after times, or checking time left out. Before and after times for one task, including checking, with weekly minutes saved. Also says where the saved time will go. Private details Customer addresses, card numbers or private contract details went into AI. Questions were summarized in the owner's own words; no private details shared. Private details were also removed from documents before summarizing. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should your "AI way" time include?
options: Only the time AI took to write
The time to check and fix AI's work too
The time you spent at lunch
check.why: Checking and fixing are part of the real time cost.

check.q: You save 4 minutes on a task you do 10 times a week. What do you write in your log?
check.why: 4 minutes times 10 times a week is 40 minutes.
